title: Zero rational rank implies torsion
statement: Let $G$ be an abelian group and put $\operatorname{rrk}(G) [def-trf-rational-rank]=\dim_{\mathbf Q}(G\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q)$. If $\operatorname{rrk}(G)=0$, then $G$ is torsion: for every $g\in G$ there is an integer $n\geq1$ with $n\,g=0$.

source.place: §2.1, Lemma 2.1.2 notation and Proposition 4.3.1 proof, p. 27: the Abhyankar bound gives E=0, “in particular, the group G ... is a torsion group”; local archival copy unavailable.

proof.text: Put $V=G\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$. By [def-trf-rational-rank], the hypothesis says $\dim_{\mathbf Q}V=0$. Thus $V=0$: if $v\ne0$, the singleton $\{v\}$ is linearly independent, since $av=0$ with $a\ne0$ implies $v=a^{-1}(av)=0$. The supremum of the cardinalities of linearly independent subsets (the vector-space dimension) would then be at least $1$, a contradiction. This argument uses cardinal dimension, not the natural-number-valued finrank of a possibly infinite-dimensional space.

source.place: Elementary singleton argument using the definition of dimension; rational rank as in the item source, Temkin §2.1 (local archival copy unavailable).

proof.text: Let $S=\mathbf Z\setminus\{0\}$, a multiplicative subset, and form $S^{-1}G$ and $S^{-1}\mathbf Z$ by [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. Identify $S^{-1}\mathbf Z$ with $\mathbf Q$ via $a/s\mapsto a/s$: every rational is such a fraction, and two such fractions are equal precisely when $at=bs$. In the localization equality criterion, $u(at-bs)=0$ for a nonzero integer $u$ is equivalent to $at=bs$ because $\mathbf Z$ is a domain. The fraction addition and multiplication formulas agree. Hence this is a ring isomorphism, compatible with the scalar action, and the map $\mathbf Z\to\mathbf Q$ is $a\mapsto a/1$.

source.place: Tag 07JZ (definition-localization-module), preceding fraction construction, specialized to the module Z; elementary rational-fraction identification.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-localization-tensor-over-base] with $R=A=\mathbf Z$, $T=S$, $M=\mathbf Z$ and $N=G$. It gives the isomorphism $S^{-1}(\mathbf Z\otimes_{\mathbf Z}G)\longrightarrow S^{-1}\mathbf Z\otimes_{\mathbf Z}G$ sending $(a\otimes g)/s$ to $(a/s)\otimes g$. The tensor universal property [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] gives mutually inverse maps $\mathbf Z\otimes_{\mathbf Z}G\rightleftarrows G$, $a\otimes g\mapsto ag$ and $g\mapsto1\otimes g$: the composite on pure tensors is $1\otimes ag=a\otimes g$, and pure tensors generate. Localizing these inverse maps using [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] gives inverse maps $S^{-1}(\mathbf Z\otimes G)\rightleftarrows S^{-1}G$. Likewise $q\otimes g\mapsto g\otimes q$ and $g\otimes q\mapsto q\otimes g$ are inverse maps by the same tensor universal property. Combining these maps and Step 2 yields an additive isomorphism $\theta:S^{-1}G\longrightarrow G\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$ with $\theta(g/s)=g\otimes(1/s)$; in particular $\theta(g/1)=g\otimes1$. Step 1 therefore implies $S^{-1}G=0$.

source.place: Tag 00DK (lemma-tensor-localization); existing general base-ring tensor-localization leaf, with the unit and symmetry maps written out.

proof.text: For any $g\in G$, Step 3 gives $g/1=0$ in $S^{-1}G$. The kernel criterion explicitly stated in [def-weil-pbc-module-localization] gives $s\in S$ with $sg=0$, so $s$ is a nonzero integer. Take $n=|s|\geq1$. If $s>0$, then $n=s$ and $ng=0$; if $s<0$, then $n=-s$ and $ng=-(sg)=0$. This proves the required elementwise torsion assertion; the annihilating integer may depend on $g$.
